blocks.text: A 24-year-old man arrives drowsy and breathing deeply and fast. His capillary glucose is far above the meter's range. Within minutes a blood gas and a set of electrolytes will tell you how acidic he is and why, and a single calculation from three numbers on the printout will show that unmeasured acid is present.

blocks.markdown: **Interpretation of biochemistry means reading numbers in context.** Urea and electrolytes (U&E) report sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and often an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which is calculated from creatinine, age and sex and is unreliable in acute kidney injury, extremes of muscle mass and pregnancy. Liver function tests (LFTs) report bilirubin, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and albumin. Troponin is a cardiac muscle protein released when myocardium is injured. Reference ranges differ between laboratories and populations, so use the range printed on the report; the typical adult reference ranges quoted in teaching are only a guide. Always ask whether the result fits the patient and whether the sample could be wrong.

blocks.caption: Anion gap (AG) estimates unmeasured anions, and adjusted calcium corrects for low albumin. Some laboratories include potassium in the anion gap and use different adjustments, so check local practice and reference ranges.

Acute or chronic kidney injury, drugs (ACE inhibitors, spironolactone), acidosis, haemolysed sample

blocks.title: Calculating and interpreting an anion gap
blocks.prompt: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes has Na 134 mmol/L, Cl 96 mmol/L and bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, with glucose and ketones raised. Calculate the anion gap and interpret it.

steps.text: Recall the formula. AG = Na - Cl - HCO3 when potassium is not included.
Compare with the reference range. A typical adult reference range without potassium is about 8 to 16 mmol/L but is laboratory dependent, so 28 is clearly raised.

Interpret. A raised anion gap with a low bicarbonate indicates a metabolic acidosis from accumulation of unmeasured acids, here ketoacids in diabetic ketoacidosis. A normal-gap acidosis would point instead to bicarbonate loss, for example from diarrhoea or renal tubular acidosis.

blocks.answer: The anion gap is 28 mmol/L, raised, consistent with ketoacidosis; always confirm with ketones, a blood gas and clinical context.

blocks.title: Adjusting calcium for albumin
blocks.prompt: A hospital patient has total calcium 2.05 mmol/L and albumin 24 g/L. What is the adjusted calcium and what does it mean?

steps.text: Recall why adjustment is needed. About half of circulating calcium is bound mainly to albumin, so low albumin lowers the total calcium without changing the physiologically active ionised fraction.
Use the formula. Adjusted Ca = 2.05 + 0.02 x (40 - 24) = 2.05 + 0.32 = 2.37 mmol/L.
Compare with the reference range. A typical adult range is roughly 2.2 to 2.6 mmol/L, laboratory dependent, so 2.37 is normal.

Interpret and caveat. The apparent hypocalcaemia is due to hypoalbuminaemia. The formula is an approximation and is unreliable in critical illness and kidney disease, where ionised calcium measurement is better.

blocks.answer: Adjusted calcium is 2.37 mmol/L, within the typical range, so the low total calcium reflects the low albumin.

blocks.markdown: **Liver tests and troponin.** A **hepatocellular** pattern has ALT and AST much higher than ALP, reflecting hepatocyte injury (viral hepatitis, drugs, alcohol, ischaemia). A **cholestatic** pattern has ALP and GGT raised out of proportion to ALT, with or without raised bilirubin, reflecting bile flow obstruction inside or outside the liver; ultrasound is the usual first imaging test for dilated bile ducts. Albumin and the INR reflect synthetic function but are affected by many non-hepatic factors. **High-sensitivity troponin** is measured on a specific assay with an assay-specific 99th percentile upper reference limit. A diagnosis of acute myocardial injury requires a rise and/or fall with at least one value above that limit; acute myocardial infarction additionally needs evidence of ischaemia. Troponin can be raised in sepsis, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, myocarditis and kidney disease, so a high value is not itself proof of coronary occlusion.

ALT and AST markedly raised, ALP mildly raised
Viral hepatitis, drug-induced injury, alcohol, ischaemic hepatitis
History, viral serology, medication review, ultrasound

ALP and GGT raised, bilirubin often raised
Gallstones, pancreatic or biliary tumour, primary biliary cholangitis, drugs
Ultrasound for dilated ducts, then MRCP or CT as indicated

Urgent clinical assessment; interpret with caution in sepsis and nutrition

blocks.title: Reading serial troponin results
blocks.prompt: A 70-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease has chest discomfort. Using an assay with a 99th percentile of 14 ng/L, her high-sensitivity troponin is 48 ng/L at presentation and 49 ng/L 3 hours later. How do you interpret this?

steps.text: Compare with the limit. Both values exceed 14 ng/L, so troponin is elevated, indicating myocardial injury.
Look for a dynamic change. The two values differ by 1 ng/L, which is within analytical and biological variation and no significant rise or fall.

Interpret. A persistently raised but static value suggests chronic myocardial injury, commonly seen in chronic kidney disease, rather than a new acute event, but the decision uses the assay-specific delta criteria and the clinical picture.
State the caveat. A single set of results never replaces clinical assessment and ECG; a patient with a compelling ischaemic history may still need further serial testing and specialist review.

blocks.answer: Elevated but unchanging troponin suggests chronic myocardial injury rather than an acute rise or fall; interpretation uses assay-specific criteria and the clinical picture.

blocks.markdown: **Reference intervals, biological variation and test performance.** A **reference interval** is usually the central 95% of values in a healthy reference population, so 5% of healthy people lie outside it for any single test and the more independent tests are requested, the more likely at least one is flagged. If each test has a 95% chance of being normal in a healthy person and the tests are independent, the chance that all *n* are normal is $0.95^n$. **Biological variation** is the natural fluctuation of an analyte in one person over time (within-individual, CV_I) and the variation between people (between-individual). Together with the analytical variation of the measurement (CV_A), these determine the **reference change value**, the percentage change between two serial results that is unlikely to be chance. **Sensitivity** is the proportion of people with disease who test positive and **specificity** is the proportion without disease who test negative; a test with very high sensitivity is useful for ruling out disease when negative.

blocks.caption: A change between two results smaller than the reference change value may be due to analytical and biological variation alone.

blocks.title: Treat the patient, not the number
blocks.text: Do not act on an unexpected result without asking whether the sample is wrong, but never dismiss a result without checking the patient. A high potassium in an unwell patient with ECG changes or kidney injury is real until proved otherwise. If doubt exists, repeat promptly and speak to the laboratory.

points: Interpret U&E, LFTs and troponin together with the clinical picture and the laboratory's own reference ranges.
Anion gap = Na - Cl - HCO3 and adjusted calcium = measured calcium + 0.02 x (40 - albumin); both are approximations.
Hepatocellular injury raises ALT and AST, cholestasis raises ALP and GGT; troponin diagnosis requires a rise and/or fall, and troponin rises in many non-coronary conditions.
Reference intervals cover the central 95% of healthy people, so many tests increase the chance of a flagged result; changes smaller than the reference change value may be noise.
Spurious results arise from haemolysis, EDTA contamination, drip-arm sampling, delayed processing and identification errors.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with pneumonia and sepsis has a high-sensitivity troponin of 120 ng/L on admission and 380 ng/L 3 hours later (assay 99th percentile 14 ng/L). The ECG shows no ST elevation. What is the most accurate statement?

options.text: This proves a type 1 myocardial infarction caused by plaque rupture
The result is normal for the age of the patient
There is acute myocardial injury, and its cause must be established clinically; it is not necessarily a coronary occlusion
The result is invalid because the ECG shows no ST elevation

questions.correctOptionText: There is acute myocardial injury, and its cause must be established clinically; it is not necessarily a coronary occlusion

distractorRationale.a: Troponin shows injury, not the mechanism; sepsis is a competing cause.
distractorRationale.b: Both values far exceed the assay's upper reference limit.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a rising value above the 99th percentile shows acute myocardial injury, which sepsis can cause without coronary occlusion.
distractorRationale.d: Many infarcts have no ST elevation and troponin remains valid.

questions.explanation: A rise above the 99th percentile defines acute myocardial injury, but injury is not always from coronary plaque rupture; sepsis, hypoxia and strain can all cause it. The clinical context and ECG determine whether it is an infarction.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has jaundice, itch, pale stools and dark urine. Liver tests show ALP 520 U/L, GGT markedly raised, ALT only modestly raised and bilirubin raised. Which interpretation and first imaging test fit best?

options.text: Cholestatic pattern; ultrasound of the liver and biliary tree

questions.correctOptionText: Cholestatic pattern; ultrasound of the liver and biliary tree

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ALP and GGT out of proportion to ALT with pale stools and dark urine suggest obstructed bile flow, and ultrasound detects dilated ducts.
distractorRationale.b: ALT and AST would dominate in hepatocellular injury, and chest imaging does not assess the biliary tree.
distractorRationale.d: Synthetic failure shows low albumin or long INR; a plain film does not show the ducts.

questions.explanation: A disproportionately raised ALP and GGT with pale stools and dark urine indicates cholestasis. Ultrasound is the usual first test because it shows dilated bile ducts and gallstones without radiation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is well and has no symptoms, but his potassium is 6.9 mmol/L. The sample took 24 hours to reach the laboratory and the report notes marked haemolysis. What is the most likely explanation and appropriate action?

options.text: True severe hyperkalaemia needing no repeat
Spurious hyperkalaemia from haemolysis and delay; repeat promptly with a fresh sample and assess clinically

questions.correctOptionText: Spurious hyperkalaemia from haemolysis and delay; repeat promptly with a fresh sample and assess clinically

distractorRationale.a: Possible if the patient is unwell or has kidney disease, but the clues point to the sample.
distractorRationale.b: The value is high, not low.
distractorRationale.c: A value of 6.9 mmol/L is not normal variation and the repeat must be prompt.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: haemolysis and delay release intracellular potassium, so the value is likely falsely high; repeat urgently while checking the patient.

questions.explanation: Red cells contain far more potassium than plasma, so haemolysis or delayed separation falsely raises measured potassium. An unexplained high result in a well patient should be repeated promptly because a real hyperkalaemia can be dangerous.

questions.stem: A rapid test for a condition has a sensitivity of 99% and a modest specificity. Which statement about a negative result is most accurate?

options.text: It proves the patient is disease free
It makes the condition unlikely, because few diseased patients are missed
It has no value because specificity is modest
It means the test was performed incorrectly

questions.correctOptionText: It makes the condition unlikely, because few diseased patients are missed

distractorRationale.a: Proof requires near-perfect performance and is never absolute.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: high sensitivity means few false negatives, so negatives are useful for ruling out.
distractorRationale.c: Modest specificity mainly affects positive results (false positives).
distractorRationale.d: A negative result is a normal outcome of a valid test.

questions.explanation: With high sensitivity almost all patients who have the condition test positive, so a negative result makes disease unlikely. Specificity influences how reliable positives are and does not remove the value of negatives.

questions.stem: A patient's total calcium is 2.62 mmol/L and albumin is 28 g/L. Calculate the adjusted calcium in mmol/L using adjusted Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 x (40 - albumin in g/L).
questions.explanation: The albumin deficit is 40 - 28 = 12 g/L, so the correction is 0.02 x 12 = 0.24 mmol/L, giving 2.62 + 0.24 = 2.86 mmol/L. This exceeds the typical upper reference limit of about 2.6 mmol/L (laboratory dependent), so true hypercalcaemia is present and low albumin was masking its size.

questions.stem: A healthy person has 10 independent blood tests, each with a reference interval covering 95% of healthy people. What is the probability, as a percentage, that all 10 results are within their intervals?
questions.explanation: Each test has a 0.95 probability of being normal, and independence multiplies them, so the probability is 0.95^10 = 0.599, or about 59.9%. Roughly 40% of healthy people will therefore have at least one flagged result, which is why isolated minor abnormalities are interpreted in context.

questions.stem: An assay has an analytical coefficient of variation of 2% and the within-person biological coefficient of variation is 6%. Calculate the reference change value for 95% confidence (Z = 1.96) as a percentage.
questions.explanation: RCV = sqrt(2) x 1.96 x sqrt(2^2 + 6^2) = 1.414 x 1.96 x sqrt(40) = 1.414 x 1.96 x 6.325 = 17.5%. A change in serial results smaller than this may be explained by analytical and biological variation rather than a true change.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman on an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone is dehydrated after vomiting. U&E show sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, urea 22 mmol/L and creatinine 240 micromol/L (baseline 85 micromol/L). Interpret the results and state your immediate considerations.
markingGuide: Acute kidney injury shown by creatinine rise from baseline and raised urea
Likely pre-renal cause from dehydration, aggravated by ACE inhibitor and spironolactone
Hyperkalaemia requires an ECG and repeat to exclude a spurious result
Hyponatraemia assessed by volume status
Review nephrotoxic and potassium-raising drugs
Check urine output and consider obstruction with ultrasound if it does not improve
eGFR unreliable in AKI
questions.explanation: The pattern is an acute rise in creatinine and urea on a background of volume depletion and drugs that reduce renal perfusion and raise potassium. Immediate considerations are confirming the result, assessing the patient and ECG, and addressing reversible causes.

questions.stem: Explain what a reference interval is and why a single result slightly outside it may not be abnormal. Discuss the role of biological variation and sensitivity in interpreting serial test results.
markingGuide: Reference interval is the central 95% of a healthy reference population
5% of healthy people fall outside for any single test
More tests increase chance of at least one flagged result
Differences between laboratories, methods and populations
Biological variation within and between individuals and analytical variation
Reference change value indicates a significant serial change
Sensitivity and specificity influence reliability of positives and negatives
Interpret with the clinical context
questions.explanation: Reference intervals describe healthy variation rather than disease thresholds, so slightly abnormal values are common. Serial comparison uses the reference change value and the performance characteristics of the test.

questions.stem: Describe five causes of spurious biochemistry results, how each arises, and how you could recognise and avoid it.
markingGuide: Haemolysis: falsely high potassium and AST; check haemolysis index; careful collection
EDTA contamination: very high potassium, very low calcium and ALP; order of draw
Drip-arm contamination: diluted or contaminated results; sample from the opposite arm
Delayed separation: falsely high potassium, low glucose; prompt transport
Wrong-patient or mislabelled sample: results that do not fit the patient; positive patient identification
Interference such as lipaemia, biotin, heterophile antibodies
Repeat and discuss with the laboratory when the result does not fit the clinical picture
questions.explanation: Spurious results arise before, during or after the analytical phase and are recognised by results that do not fit the clinical picture. Prevention depends on correct collection, labelling and transport, and communication with the laboratory.
